curations.original_notes: prayer before God
curations.textual_observation: Psalm 22 is a lament addressed to God, moving from complaint toward trust and praise.
curations.uncertainty: Psalm 22 is a lament with petition and praise; the Psalter includes forms beyond prayer and should not be reduced to one genre.
curations.why: The psalm gives a concrete example of prayer language.

curations.original_notes: Psalms in worship
curations.textual_observation: Psalm 118:19–29 depicts entry through the gates, thanksgiving, and blessing in worship.
curations.uncertainty: Psalm 118 frames worship in a specific liturgical poem; the practice and setting should not be generalized to every psalm.
curations.why: This passage illustrates a liturgical use of the Psalms without implying that every psalm served the same setting.

curations.original_notes: prayerful wisdom
curations.textual_observation: Psalm 1 portrays the blessed person meditating on YHWH’s instruction and contrasts that way with the wicked.
curations.uncertainty: Psalm 1 frames a life shaped by instruction and meditation; not every psalm is a wisdom poem or prayer of the same kind.
curations.why: It illustrates wisdom as a life shaped by Torah; the psalm itself does not identify its genre as wisdom or prayer.

curations.original_notes: explicit rereading of earlier Scripture
curations.textual_observation: Hebrews 1:1–4 contrasts God’s former speech through prophets with speech “in a Son” and describes the Son’s exalted status.
curations.uncertainty: Hebrews rereads Israel's Scriptures within its own argument; the link does not mean every canonical reading is a direct prediction.
curations.why: This passage illustrates Hebrews’ canonical framing, but these verses do not quote a particular earlier Scripture.

curations.original_notes: fulfillment citations

supporting_ckl_sources.author: Holmes, Michael W., editor
supporting_ckl_sources.title: The Greek New Testament: SBL Edition, Matthew

curations.textual_observation: Matthew 1:22–23 presents Jesus’ conception as fulfilling what the Lord spoke through the prophet and quotes the Emmanuel saying.
curations.uncertainty: Matthew explicitly introduces a fulfillment citation; the link concerns Matthew's reception of Isaiah and does not settle the original passage's sole meaning.
curations.why: Matthew explicitly relates its infancy narrative to prophetic wording; this does not settle Isaiah’s original oracle’s only possible referent.

curations.original_notes: faith receives God's verdict
curations.textual_observation: Galatians 2:15–21 contrasts justification by works of law with justification through faith in/of Jesus Christ.
curations.uncertainty: Galatians connects faith and justification in a disputed Pauline argument; the curation does not reduce faith to assent or settle every theological debate.
curations.why: The passage links justification and faith; leave the debated translation of pistis Christou unresolved.

curations.original_notes: righteous standing before God
curations.textual_observation: Galatians 2:15–21 argues that a person is not justified by works of law and describes life in Christ.
curations.uncertainty: The relation between justification and righteousness is theological and lexical; traditions differ over how Paul develops it in Galatians.
curations.why: This supports a relationship between justification and righteousness-language while avoiding a broad doctrinal definition from one passage.

curations.original_notes: Hebrews explains fulfillment
curations.textual_observation: Hebrews 9:11–14 presents Christ as high priest entering the greater sanctuary with his own blood and cleansing the conscience.
curations.uncertainty: Hebrews interprets sacrifice through its own priestly and covenant argument; it should not erase the distinct ritual settings of Torah.
curations.why: The passage shows Hebrews’ sacrificial argument; it should not stand in for the Bible’s full range of sacrifice.

curations.original_notes: organized sacrificial practice
curations.textual_observation: Leviticus 1:1–17 gives instructions for burnt offerings from herd, flock, and birds.
curations.uncertainty: Leviticus describes particular offerings and priestly procedures; biblical sacrifice includes more than one rite or purpose.
curations.why: This is one prescribed offering within the larger sacrificial system, not a complete account of every sacrifice.

curations.original_notes: judgment does not cancel hope
curations.textual_observation: 1 Thessalonians 5:1–11 describes the day of the Lord as unexpected and pairs warning with salvation, faith, love, and hope.
curations.uncertainty: First Thessalonians joins expectation of judgment with encouragement and hope; the passage does not support date-setting.
curations.why: The passage supports hope amid judgment without speculation about dates.

curations.original_notes: breath/spirit term
curations.textual_observation: Acts 2:1–4 describes a sound like a rushing wind and the disciples’ filling with the Holy Spirit; the Greek text uses pnoē for the sound and pneuma for Spirit.
curations.uncertainty: Greek pneuma also has a range of breath, wind, and spirit senses; Hebrew ruach and Greek pneuma are not etymologically interchangeable.
curations.why: The distinction prevents wind imagery and the pneuma word study from being conflated.

curations.original_notes: theology of the Spirit
curations.textual_observation: John 14:16–26 calls the Spirit the Advocate and Spirit of truth and says the Spirit will teach and remind the disciples.
curations.uncertainty: John's farewell discourse presents the Paraclete in Johannine language; it is distinct from Luke's Pentecost narrative.
curations.why: These verses provide a specific basis for the pneumatology connection.

curations.original_notes: revelation's critique of empire

supporting_ckl_sources.author: Steven J. Friesen
supporting_ckl_sources.title: Imperial Cults and the Apocalypse of John

supporting_ckl_sources.author: Craig R. Koester
supporting_ckl_sources.title: Revelation: A New Translation with Introduction and Commentary

supporting_ckl_sources.author: Craig R. Koester, editor
supporting_ckl_sources.title: The Oxford Handbook of the Book of Revelation

curations.textual_observation: Revelation 13:1–10 portrays a beast receiving authority and demanding worship; scholars have read the imagery against Roman imperial power, though its referents remain debated.
curations.uncertainty: Revelation's beasts and Babylon have long been read in relation to Rome, but the imagery is symbolic and scholarly readings of its political referents differ.
curations.why: The secondary sources support an interpretive imperial-context reading, not an uncontested identification of every symbol.

curations.original_notes: theology of the Spirit
curations.textual_observation: Acts 2:1–21 narrates the Spirit’s outpouring and Peter’s citation of Joel to interpret the event.
curations.uncertainty: Acts 2 is one narrative of the Spirit's activity; the curation does not collapse biblical imagery into a single later doctrine.
curations.why: The passage gives a concrete account of the Spirit’s significance in Acts’ mission narrative.

curations.original_notes: rest after deliverance
curations.textual_observation: Deuteronomy 5:12–15 grounds Sabbath rest in Israel’s memory of slavery and deliverance from Egypt.
curations.uncertainty: Deuteronomy grounds Sabbath rest in Israel's liberation from Egypt; the curation does not equate Sabbath and Exodus in every biblical setting.
curations.why: The text links Sabbath observance with the Exodus pattern through rest for servants and household members.

curations.original_notes: redemption pattern
curations.textual_observation: In 1 Corinthians 10:1–11 Paul presents Israel’s wilderness experiences as examples and warnings for the Corinthian community.
curations.uncertainty: Paul explicitly uses the Exodus generation as an example for the Corinthian community; later typological theory should not be collapsed into every form of intertextuality.
curations.why: This is an explicit later scriptural reuse of the Exodus generation as a pattern for instruction.

curations.original_notes: Paul on Abraham
curations.textual_observation: Romans 4:1–25 uses Abraham’s faith and Genesis 15:6 to argue about justification before circumcision.
curations.uncertainty: Romans 4 is Paul's reception of Abraham; it should not be substituted for the narrative context of Genesis or treated as the only Jewish reading.
curations.why: This is Paul’s interpretation of Abraham in the argument of Romans, rather than a summary biography.

curations.original_notes: promise carried forward
curations.textual_observation: Matthew 1:1–17 opens by identifying Jesus as Messiah, son of David and son of Abraham, and traces his genealogy.
curations.uncertainty: Matthew frames its genealogy with Abraham and David, but its omissions and structure make it more than a continuous list of every generation.
curations.why: The genealogy foregrounds lineage and messianic identity; the passage does not explain every genealogy’s purpose.
